title: Episode 64: The Hatfield-McCoy Feud: Blood and Timber in the Tug Valley
description:
The Hatfield-McCoy Feud: Blood and Timber in the Tug Valley: How a dispute over a razorback hog and Civil War loyalties ignited America's most famous family blood vendetta. Join Rebecca and George for an immersive historical deep dive into this extraordinary chapter of the American story.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome back to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. In the steep, shadowed hollows of the Tug River Valley along the border of Kentucky and West Virginia, two proud mountain clans waged the most famous and mythologized family feud in American history: the Hatfield-McCoy vendetta. What popular culture remembers as a cartoonish brawl over a stolen pig was, in reality, a deadly clash of Civil War allegiances, industrial timber monopolies, political corruption, and frontier vengeance. Over nearly three decades, the feud claimed a dozen lives, brought two sovereign states to the brink of armed warfare, and culminated in a sensational midnight house burning. George tells the true, tragic story of the Hatfields and McCoys.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE TWO PATRIARCHS OF THE TUG VALLEY
The Tug Fork of the Big Sandy River was a rugged, mountainous frontier separating Pike County, Kentucky, from Logan County, West Virginia. In the eighteen sixties, the valley was dominated by two powerful, sprawling extended clans. On the West Virginia side were the Hatfields, commanded by William Anderson 'Devil Anse' Hatfield. Devil Anse was a towering, heavily bearded six-foot mountaineer with sharp gray eyes, an expert marksman, and a shrewd, highly successful timber merchant who owned thousands of acres of virgin mountain timber and employed dozens of armed clansmen in his logging crews. Across the river on the Kentucky side lived the McCoys, led by Randolph 'Ole Ran'l' McCoy. Randolph was an austere, brooding, deeply religious patriarch who farmed and operated a small gristmill on Blackberry Creek. During the American Civil War, deep ideological fractures divided the families. Devil Anse Hatfield and his brothers had served as Confederate cavalrymen in the Logan County Wildcats, while Randolph McCoy and several sons served in the Union Army. In eighteen sixty-five, Randolph's brother Harmon McCoy, who had returned home after serving in the Union infantry, was murdered in an ambush; although Devil Anse's fiery Confederate uncle, Jim Vance, was widely suspected, no charges were ever filed, planting the first bitter seeds of clan resentment. The steep hollows of the Tug Valley were thick with ancient virgin timber, and both clans operated logging rafts that floated valuable oak and walnut logs downriver to market.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE TRIAL OF THE RAZORBACK HOG
Thirteen years later, in the autumn of eighteen seventy-eight, the smoldering hostility exploded into the open over a single razorback hog. In the Appalachian mountains, where livestock roamed free on the open range, pigs were identified by unique notches cut into their ears. Randolph McCoy visited the farm of Floyd Hatfield, a cousin of Devil Anse, and spotted an ear-notched hog in Hatfield's pen that Randolph adamantly claimed belonged to him. Floyd Hatfield insisted the pig was his, and Randolph brought formal legal charges of theft. The matter was tried before the local justice of the peace, Anderson 'Preacher Anse' Hatfield, Devil Anse's brother. The trial took place before a six-man Hatfield and six-man McCoy jury. The decisive witness was Bill Staton, a nephew of Randolph McCoy who was married to a Hatfield woman. Staton testified under oath that the hog's ear notches were Floyd Hatfield's marks. Based on Staton's testimony, the jury ruled in favor of the Hatfields. Randolph McCoy was humiliated and enraged, regarding Staton as a treacherous Judas. Two years later, two of Randolph's nephews, Sam and Paris McCoy, ambushed Bill Staton in the woods, shooting him dead; although tried for murder, the McCoy brothers were acquitted on grounds of self-defense, deepening the thirst for vengeance. The hog trial was held in a frontier cabin crowded with armed partisans, where every word of testimony was weighed with deadly gravity by two suspicious mountain families. Early settlers faced immense hardships carving farms and homesteads from the dense eastern woodlands, battling disease, inclement weather, and frontier isolation with unyielding resolve.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE STAR-CROSSED LOVERS OF ELECTION DAY
The feud took a romantic and tragic turn on an election day in August eighteen eighty. Johnse Hatfield, Devil Anse's handsome, reckless eighteen-year-old son, crossed the river to attend a Kentucky political rally and dance. There he met Roseanna McCoy, Randolph's beautiful, spirited twenty-year-old daughter. The two fell instantly in love and slipped away into the mountains, with Roseanna defying her family to move into the Hatfield homestead in West Virginia. Randolph McCoy was beside himself with fury, viewing his daughter's relationship with a Hatfield as the ultimate betrayal. Months later, when Johnse Hatfield ventured into Kentucky, a heavily armed McCoy posse ambushed him and took him prisoner, planning to transport him to the Pikeville jail on old warrants. Learning of her lover's capture, Roseanna mounted a horse bareback, galloped through the night across the river to alert Devil Anse, who mobilized an armed squad of twenty Hatfield riflemen. The Hatfields intercepted the McCoy posse on the road, leveled their Winchesters, and rescued Johnse without firing a shot. Yet despite Roseanna's courage, Johnse eventually abandoned her, marrying her cousin Nancy McCoy, breaking Roseanna's heart and leaving the families more bitterly divided than ever. Roseanna McCoy lived out her remaining years in quiet grief, remembered by valley elders as a brave, tender-hearted soul caught between two unyielding mountain empires. The spirit of American innovation was evident in every workshop and meeting hall, where practical mechanics and visionary thinkers sought solutions to the most challenging obstacles of their era.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE ELECTION DAY STABBING AND THE PAWPAW TREES
The point of no return arrived on August seventh, eighteen eighty-two, during another rowdy election day near Blackberry Creek, Kentucky. An argument broke out between Devil Anse's younger brother, Ellison Hatfield, and three of Randolph McCoy's sons: Tolbert, Pharmer, and young Randolph Jr. Fueled by moonshine whiskey, the brawl turned violent. Tolbert McCoy drew a pocketknife, stabbing Ellison multiple times. As Ellison fought back, pinning Tolbert to the ground, Pharmer McCoy pulled a revolver and shot Ellison through the lungs. Kentucky constables arrested the three McCoy brothers, planning to march them to Pikeville for trial. But Devil Anse Hatfield and his armed clansmen intercepted the deputies, disarmed them, and took the three McCoy boys back across the river to West Virginia, locking them in an abandoned schoolhouse. Devil Anse issued a cold ultimatum: if Ellison lived, the McCoy boys would be surrendered to Kentucky courts; if Ellison died, they would pay with their lives. Two days later, Ellison Hatfield succumbed to his wounds. On the night of August ninth, the Hatfields marched the three bound McCoy brothers back to the Kentucky bank of the Tug River, tied them to pawpaw bushes, and executed them with a firing squad of over fifty rifle shots. The execution at the pawpaw bushes cast a permanent pall of dread over the Tug Valley, forcing families to sleep with loaded rifles across their knees for years. News of these extraordinary events traveled by telegraph and steam train across the nation, captivating readers in major eastern cities and inspiring future generations of pioneers and inventors.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE PIKEVILLE LAWYER AND THE BOUNTY HUNTERS
The brutal execution of the three McCoy boys shocked the state of Kentucky. A brilliant, ambitious Pikeville attorney named Perry Cline, who was related to the McCoys and held an old financial grievance against Devil Anse Hatfield over a disputed timber land settlement, launched a legal crusade. Cline used his political influence in the state capital of Frankfort to convince Kentucky Governor Simon Bolivar Buckner to issue formal extradition warrants and post massive bounties for Devil Anse and twenty Hatfield clansmen. To hunt down the Hatfields, Cline recruited 'Bad Frank' Phillips, a fearless, ruthless former deputy sheriff who organized a heavily armed paramilitary posse of bounty hunters. Phillips launched illegal cross-border raids into West Virginia, raiding Hatfield farms, engaging in running gun battles, and kidnapping clan members to collect the state bounties. West Virginia Governor E. Willis Wilson retaliated by deploying the West Virginia state militia to protect his citizens, threatening to march armed troops into Kentucky. The two sovereign American states were on the verge of interstate civil war, with federal marshals struggling to maintain peace along the border. Governors in Frankfort and Charleston traded angry diplomatic dispatches, while sensational yellow journalism in New York painted the mountain people as lawless savages. The enduring lessons of this historic chapter continue to resonate across American culture, reminding us of the courage, sacrifice, and vision of those who shaped the destiny of our nation.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE NEW YEAR'S NIGHT MASSACRE
Desperate to end the legal harassment once and for all, a rogue faction of the Hatfield clan, led by the ruthless Cap Hatfield and uncle Jim Vance, decided to wipe out the McCoy family leadership. In the freezing early morning hours of January first, eighteen eighty-eight, the Hatfield squad surrounded Randolph McCoy's isolated log cabin on Blackberry Creek. When Randolph refused to surrender, the raiders set the cabin roof on fire with torches. As the family rushed into the yard in their nightclothes through the smoke, the gunmen opened fire: Randolph's grown daughter Alifair was shot through the heart, his son Calvin was cut down by rifle fire, and his wife Sarah was bludgeoned with a shotgun barrel, leaving her skull fractured. Randolph McCoy managed to shoot his way through the circle of fire, escaping barefoot into the snowy woods. The cold-blooded murder of innocent women and children repulsed public opinion across the nation, and Bad Frank Phillips's posse relentlessly hunted down the perpetrators. Jim Vance was cornered in the mountains and killed in a shootout, and eight Hatfields were captured and brought in heavy chains to the Pikeville jail. The New Year massacre marked the tragic nadir of the conflict, demonstrating the catastrophic cost of unbridled vengeance when law and reason are abandoned.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE SCAFFOLD IN PIKEVILLE AND THE TRUCE
The feud culminated in eighteen eighty-nine when the Supreme Court of the United States ruled in Mahon v. Justice that Kentucky had legal jurisdiction to try the captured Hatfields, even though they had been illegally kidnapped from West Virginia soil. In eighteen ninety, following high-profile trials in Pikeville, seven Hatfields were sentenced to life imprisonment, and Ellison Mounts—believed to be Ellison Hatfield's illegitimate son who had shot Alifair McCoy—was publicly hanged before a crowd of thousands on the courthouse square in Pikeville. Devil Anse Hatfield, recognizing that the era of frontier clannish isolation was ending as coal and railroad companies bought up the mountains, retired to an isolated homestead on Island Creek, West Virginia, where he was baptized in a mountain stream at age seventy-three. In nineteen twenty-one, Devil Anse passed away peacefully of pneumonia at eighty-one; a life-sized Carrara marble statue imported from Italy marks his grave. Finally, in June two thousand and three, over sixty descendants of both families gathered in Pikeville to sign an official proclamation of peace, formally ending the bloodiest family feud in American lore and proving that even the deepest historical hatreds can ultimately yield to forgiveness, shared heritage, and peace. Today, descendants of the Hatfields and McCoys celebrate their shared Appalachian heritage together, proving that reconciliation and forgiveness are always possible.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
The Hatfield-McCoy feud was a tragic clash of frontier loyalties and human passions that became an immortal American legend. I'm Rebecca. Join us next week for another compelling journey into the hidden chapters of our past.
